3.13.39 Activity projection

Do not write user-facing activity separately from audit manually in every route.

Use:

Domain Event
      ↓
Outbox
      ↓
Activity Projector
      ↓
agreement_activity

This maintains the architecture established in 3.11.

3.13.40 Obligation versioning

Obligations themselves should be immutable in their contractual meaning once activated.

For a significant change:

Old obligation
     ↓
SUPERSEDED
     ↓
New obligation

rather than:

UPDATE title
UPDATE frequency
UPDATE due date

without history.

Operational fields such as assignment can change without superseding the legal source.

3.13.41 No hardcoded contractual rules

Do not write code such as:

days_until_due = 30

or:

frequency = "MONTHLY"

unless it is explicitly an application-level configuration for non-contractual behavior.

Contractual data must be:

stored
configured
selected
or explicitly entered

For example:

recurrence_rule = actual_obligation.recurrence_rule

not:

recurrence_rule = {
    "frequency": "MONTHLY"
}
3.13.42 Extraction architecture for future AI

Later, a real document parser/AI service can produce:

Agreement
   ↓
Document extraction
   ↓
Candidate obligation
   ↓
confidence + source location
   ↓
human review
   ↓
ACTIVE obligation

Candidate:

{
  "title": "Submit quarterly report",
  "candidate_due_rule": {
    "frequency": "QUARTERLY"
  },
  "source": {
    "document_id": "...",
    "page": 14,
    "block_reference": "..."
  },
  "confidence": 0.94,
  "status": "REVIEW_REQUIRED"
}

The 0.94 is model output, not contractual truth.

The obligation becomes authoritative only after verification.

3.14 — Contract Risk, Clause Intelligence & Obligation Risk Detection

This is the intelligence layer on top of the agreement system.

The fundamental separation is:

Contract source
    ↓
Observed facts
    ↓
Analysis
    ↓
Risk findings
    ↓
Human decision

Never:

AI analysis → contract truth

An AI model can say:

“This clause appears to create an uncapped liability exposure.”

It cannot silently modify the clause, declare the contract legally invalid, or mark an obligation as breached.

3.14.1 What this milestone adds

The system will detect and track:

Clause risks
Missing terms
Contradictory terms
Ambiguous terms
Unusually broad obligations
Uncapped liability
Unclear termination rights
Unbalanced indemnification
Weak notice provisions
Renewal risks
Payment risks
Data/privacy-related clauses
Security obligations
Insurance requirements
Service-level commitments
Unusual deadlines
Obligation concentration
Evidence gaps
Version-to-version risk changes

The actual checks available depend on the rules configured for the workspace and agreement type.

There should be no universal claim that a particular clause is “legally bad.”

                    ┌─────────────────────┐
                    │ Agreement Version   │
                    └──────────┬──────────┘

      └──────┬───────┘  └──────┬───────┘  └──────┬────────┘

3.14.3 Three analysis engines

Do not make an LLM responsible for everything.

Use three complementary engines.

Engine A — Deterministic rules

Best for facts like:

liability_cap_missing
expiry_date_missing
renewal_term_missing
required_party_missing
notice_period_missing
evidence_requirement_missing

These should be extremely reliable.

Engine B — Semantic analysis

Useful for:

ambiguous language
contradictory obligations
broad discretion
unusual commitments
potentially one-sided provisions

This is where NLP/LLM analysis is useful.

Engine C — Version comparison

Detect:

risk introduced
risk removed
risk increased
risk decreased
clause materially changed
obligation materially changed

This is especially important after amendments.

3.14.7 Evidence is mandatory

A finding without source evidence should not be treated as a production-quality finding.

Every finding needs something like:

{
  "version_id": "...",
  "block_id": "...",
  "source_reference": {
    "block_id": "...",
    "field_path": "...",
    "document_id": null
  },
  "excerpt_hash": "..."
}

For a rule such as “expiry date missing”:

{
  "source": {
    "type": "LIFECYCLE_ANALYSIS",
    "version_id": "..."
  },
  "finding": {
    "missing": "EXPIRY_DATE"
  }
}

The system must never invent a quotation that does not exist in the source.

3.14.8 Risk rules

Rules should live in data/configuration, not scattered across controllers.

Create:

class RiskRule(Base):
    __tablename__ = "risk_rules"

    id = mapped_column(
        String(255),
        primary_key=True,
    )

    organization_id = mapped_column(
        PGUUID(as_uuid=True),
        ForeignKey(
            "organizations.id",
            ondelete="CASCADE",
        ),
        nullable=False,
    )

    agreement_type_id = mapped_column(
        PGUUID(as_uuid=True),
        ForeignKey("agreement_types.id"),
    )

    name = mapped_column(
        String(500),
        nullable=False,
    )

    category = mapped_column(
        String(64),
        nullable=False,
    )

    enabled = mapped_column(
        Boolean,
        nullable=False,
        default=True,
    )

    configuration = mapped_column(
        JSONB,
        nullable=False,
    )

    severity_mapping = mapped_column(
        JSONB,
        nullable=False,
    )

    version = mapped_column(
        Integer,
        nullable=False,
    )

A rule might configure:

{
  "condition": "REQUIRED_TERM_MISSING",
  "term_type": "EXPIRY_DATE"
}

The actual production configuration is created by the administrator, imported from controlled configuration, or supplied by your product rules.

3.14.9 Why not hardcode rules?

Avoid this:

if agreement_type == "SUPPLIER":
    if not expiry_date:
        ...

That becomes an unmaintainable legal-policy layer.

Prefer:

Database rule
    ↓
Rule resolver
    ↓
Applicable agreement types
    ↓
Analyzer

This lets you change policy without redeploying application code.

3.14.10 Deterministic rule engine
rules.py
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class RuleFinding:

    rule_id: str
    category: str
    severity: str
    title: str
    summary: str
    explanation: str
    evidence: dict


class DeterministicRiskEngine:

    async def analyze(
        self,
        *,
        agreement,
        version,
        lifecycle,
        obligations,
        rules,
    ) -> list[RuleFinding]:

        findings = []

        for rule in rules:

            if not rule.enabled:
                continue

            result = self._evaluate_rule(
                rule=rule,
                lifecycle=lifecycle,
                obligations=obligations,
            )

            if result:
                findings.append(result)

        return findings

    def _evaluate_rule(
        self,
        *,
        rule,
        lifecycle,
        obligations,
    ):

        config = rule.configuration
        condition = config.get("condition")

        if condition == "REQUIRED_TERM_MISSING":

            term = config.get("term_type")

            if term == "EXPIRY_DATE":
                if lifecycle.expiry_date is None:
                    return RuleFinding(
                        rule_id=rule.id,
                        category=rule.category,
                        severity=self._severity(
                            rule,
                            "MISSING",
                        ),
                        title=rule.name,
                        summary=(
                            "The configured expiry term "
                            "could not be resolved."
                        ),
                        explanation=(
                            "No verified expiry date is available "
                            "for the analyzed agreement version."
                        ),
                        evidence={
                            "source": "LIFECYCLE",
                            "term": "EXPIRY_DATE",
                        },
                    )

        return None

    @staticmethod
    def _severity(rule, key):
        mapping = rule.severity_mapping
        return mapping.get(key, "INFO")

The engine evaluates actual data.

It does not manufacture anything.

3.14.11 Semantic analysis

For semantic analysis, create an explicit interface:

class SemanticRiskAnalyzer:

    async def analyze(
        self,
        *,
        agreement_id,
        version_id,
        blocks,
        analysis_policy,
    ) -> list[dict]:

        ...

The implementation can later use:

local model
managed LLM
private inference
specialized NLP service

depending on deployment.

But the output must conform to a strict schema.

3.14.12 LLM output contract

Never directly save unrestricted model JSON.

Use structured validation:

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field


class SemanticFinding(BaseModel):

    category: str
    severity: str

    title: str

    summary: str
    explanation: str

    confidence: float = Field(
        ge=0,
        le=1,
    )

    source_references: list[dict]

    reasoning_basis: list[str]

Then validate:

finding = SemanticFinding.model_validate(
    model_output
)

Anything invalid is rejected.

3.14.13 Never trust model citations

This is extremely important.

The model might return:

{
  "source_references": [
    {
      "block_id": "wrong-id"
    }
  ]
}

The backend must verify that:

version_id exists
+
block_id exists in that version
+
reference points to real content

before saving the finding.

3.14.14 Source-grounded finding creation
async def validate_source_reference(
    document,
    reference,
):

    block_id = reference.get("block_id")

    if not block_id:
        raise ValueError(
            "Finding requires a source block"
        )

    block = find_block(
        document,
        block_id,
    )

    if block is None:
        raise ValueError(
            "Referenced source block does not exist"
        )

    return block

This prevents hallucinated evidence from becoming stored intelligence.

3.14.15 Risk scoring

Risk severity and confidence are separate.

For example:

Severity: HIGH
Confidence: LOW

means:

The potential impact may be high, but the analyzer isn't sufficiently certain.

That is very different from:

Severity: LOW
Confidence: HIGH

Create a scoring service.

class RiskScoringService:

    def calculate(
        self,
        *,
        impact: float,
        likelihood: float,
        confidence: float,
    ) -> int:

        impact = self._clamp(impact)
        likelihood = self._clamp(likelihood)
        confidence = self._clamp(confidence)

        raw = (
            impact
            * likelihood
            * confidence
            * 100
        )

        return round(raw)

    @staticmethod
    def _clamp(value):
        return max(
            0.0,
            min(1.0, float(value)),
        )

Do not claim the resulting number is objective legal risk.

Call it:

System risk score

and expose how it was calculated.

3.14.16 Score explanation

Store:

{
  "impact": 0.9,
  "likelihood": 0.7,
  "confidence": 0.91,
  "score": 57,
  "scoring_policy_version": 3
}

Then the user can inspect why the score changed.

3.14.17 Risk bands

Use configurable thresholds:

class RiskBandResolver:

    def resolve(
        self,
        score: int,
        thresholds: dict,
    ) -> str:

        critical = thresholds["critical"]
        high = thresholds["high"]
        medium = thresholds["medium"]
        low = thresholds["low"]

        if score >= critical:
            return "CRITICAL"

        if score >= high:
            return "HIGH"

        if score >= medium:
            return "MEDIUM"

        if score >= low:
            return "LOW"

        return "INFO"

Again, thresholds are policy/configuration.

3.14.18 Contradiction detection

One of the highest-value features is finding conflicts inside the agreement.

Example concept:

Clause A:
Payment due within 30 days.

Clause B:
Payment due within 45 days.

The engine should generate:

Potential contradiction
Confidence: HIGH

with both source references:

{
  "references": [
    {
      "block_id": "..."
    },
    {
      "block_id": "..."
    }
  ]
}

The system should not automatically decide which clause wins.

3.14.19 Cross-clause analyzer
class CrossClauseAnalyzer:

    async def analyze(

        # Semantic comparison implementation

This engine should compare actual clauses, not summaries produced by another model.

3.14.20 Obligation risk integration

3.13 already knows:

obligation
deadline
responsible party
evidence
exception
performance

3.14 can therefore detect operational risk.

Examples:

Repeated late fulfillment
High number of open exceptions
Missing evidence
Upcoming obligation with no owner
Obligation sourced from ambiguous clause
Obligation depends on missing lifecycle term

Example finding:

HIGH
Repeated obligation delays

7 of the last 9 instances were completed after the recorded due date.

That statement must be generated from actual instance records.

3.14.21 Obligation risk analyzer
class ObligationRiskAnalyzer:

    async def analyze(
        self,
        *,
        obligation,
        instances,
    ):

        if not instances:
            return None

        completed = [
            x for x in instances
            if x.completed_at is not None
        ]

        if not completed:
            return None

        late = [
            x for x in completed
            if x.due_at
            and x.completed_at > x.due_at
        ]

        late_ratio = len(late) / len(completed)

        if late_ratio < 0.5:
            return None

        return {
            "category": "OBLIGATION",
            "severity": "HIGH",
            "title": "Repeated late obligation completion",
            "summary": (
                "Recorded obligation performance shows "
                "a high rate of late completion."
            ),
            "metrics": {
                "completed_instances": len(completed),
                "late_instances": len(late),
                "late_ratio": late_ratio,
            },
        }

This is an operational observation, not a legal conclusion.

3.14.29 Background task
tasks.py
from celery import shared_task


@shared_task(
    bind=True,
    autoretry_for=(Exception,),
    retry_backoff=True,
    max_retries=5,
)
def analyze_agreement_risk(
    self,
    agreement_id: str,
    version_id: str,
):

    import asyncio

    asyncio.run(
        _analyze(
            agreement_id,
            version_id,
        )
    )


async def _analyze(
    agreement_id: str,
    version_id: str,
):

    from app.db.session import async_session_factory
    from .service import RiskAnalysisService

    async with async_session_factory() as db:

        service = RiskAnalysisService()

        await service.analyze_version(
            db=db,
            agreement_id=agreement_id,
            version_id=version_id,
        )

        await db.commit()

3.14.33 Overall agreement risk

Do not simply:

max(finding.score)

and call it “risk.”

Instead use a configurable aggregation policy.

Example:

class RiskAggregationService:

    def aggregate(
        self,
        findings,
        policy,
    ):

        if not findings:
            return {
                "score": None,
                "band": None,
            }

        weighted = sum(
            f.score * self._weight(f, policy)
            for f in findings
            if f.status not in {
                "DISMISSED",
                "SUPERSEDED",
            }
        )

        denominator = sum(
            self._weight(f, policy)
            for f in findings
            if f.status not in {
                "DISMISSED",
                "SUPERSEDED",
            }
        )

        if denominator == 0:
            return {
                "score": None,
                "band": None,
            }

        score = round(
            weighted / denominator
        )

        return {
            "score": score,
            "band": self._band(score, policy),
        }

    def _weight(self, finding, policy):
        return policy["category_weights"].get(
            finding.category,
            1,
        )

The aggregation policy should itself have a version.

3.14.34 Do not hide uncertainty

The UI should show:

Risk: HIGH
Confidence: MEDIUM
Source: Semantic analysis

not just:

HIGH

For AI-generated findings:

should be visible.

3.14.50 Failed analysis

Never discard the agreement because analysis fails.

The states are independent:

Agreement:
APPROVED

Risk analysis:
FAILED

Then notify the appropriate user.

The agreement's legal/workflow state should not be arbitrarily changed just because the intelligence subsystem failed.

A configured risk gate can prevent a signing transition when required analysis is unavailable, but that is a deliberate policy decision.

3.15 — Contract Obligation Intelligence, Automated Monitoring & External Data Verification

This milestone connects obligations to real external systems and verifiable external evidence so the platform can detect when contractual commitments are actually being fulfilled or falling behind.

The key architecture remains:

Contractual obligation
        ↓
Configured monitoring rule
        ↓
Authorized external source
        ↓
Real observed data
        ↓
Evidence normalization
        ↓
Evaluation
        ↓
Exception / performance event
        ↓
Human review / workflow

The system must never fabricate an observation when an external source is unavailable.

3.15.1 What changes

Before 3.15:

Agreement
  ↓
Obligation
  ↓
Task
  ↓
Human enters completion/evidence

After 3.15:

Agreement
  ↓
Obligation
  ↓
Monitoring definition
  ↓
External integration
  ↓
Real observation
  ↓
Evidence
  ↓
Evaluation
  ↓
Task / Exception / Notification

Example:

A contract requires a supplier to deliver a report every month.

The platform can now monitor a connected source such as:

SFTP
REST API
ERP
CRM
Cloud storage
Webhook provider
Database connector
Email ingestion
Document repository

But only when that integration has actually been configured and authorized.

3.15.2 Do not build provider-specific logic into obligations

Avoid:

if provider == "salesforce":
    ...
elif provider == "sap":
    ...

inside your obligation service.

Use an integration abstraction:

Obligation
   ↓
Monitoring Rule
   ↓
Integration Connection
   ↓
Connector
   ↓
Observation

This allows new providers without rewriting contract logic.

from enum import StrEnum


class IntegrationType(StrEnum):

    WEBHOOK = "WEBHOOK"
    SFTP = "SFTP"
    EMAIL = "EMAIL"
    DATABASE = "DATABASE"

    CONNECTING = "CONNECTING"
    ACTIVE = "ACTIVE"
    DEGRADED = "DEGRADED"
    DISCONNECTED = "DISCONNECTED"
    FAILED = "FAILED"

    DRAFT = "DRAFT"
    ACTIVE = "ACTIVE"

    DISABLED = "DISABLED"

3.15.5 Integration connection

Create a workspace-scoped integration.

# backend/app/monitoring/models.py

from datetime import datetime
from uuid import UUID, uuid4

from sqlalchemy import (
    Boolean,
    DateTime,
    ForeignKey,
    Index,
    String,
    text,
)
from sqlalchemy.dialects.postgresql import JSONB, UUID as PGUUID
from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped, mapped_column

from app.db.base import Base

from .enums import (
    IntegrationType,
    IntegrationStatus,
    MonitoringStatus,
    ObservationStatus,
    EvaluationResult,
    EvaluationStatus,
    CredentialStatus,
)


class IntegrationConnection(Base):
    __tablename__ = "integration_connections"

    id: Mapped[UUID] = mapped_column(
        PGUUID(as_uuid=True),
        primary_key=True,
        default=uuid4,
    )

    organization_id: Mapped[UUID] = mapped_column(
        PGUUID(as_uuid=True),
        ForeignKey(
            "organizations.id",
            ondelete="CASCADE",
        ),
        nullable=False,
    )

    name: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(
        String(255),
        nullable=False,
    )

    integration_type: Mapped[IntegrationType] = mapped_column(
        String(64),
        nullable=False,
    )

    provider_key: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(
        String(255),
        nullable=False,
    )

    status: Mapped[IntegrationStatus] = mapped_column(
        String(32),
        nullable=False,
    )

    configuration: Mapped[dict] = mapped_column(
        JSONB,
        nullable=False,
    )

    created_by: Mapped[UUID] = mapped_column(
        PGUUID(as_uuid=True),
        ForeignKey("users.id"),
        nullable=False,
    )

    created_at: Mapped[datetime] = mapped_column(
        DateTime(timezone=True),
        nullable=False,
        server_default=text("CURRENT_TIMESTAMP"),
    )

    updated_at: Mapped[datetime] = mapped_column(
        DateTime(timezone=True),
        nullable=False,
        server_default=text("CURRENT_TIMESTAMP"),
    )

    __table_args__ = (
        Index(
            "ix_integration_connections_org",
            "organization_id",
            "status",
        ),
    )
3.15.6 Credentials must be separate

Do not store access tokens inside ordinary configuration JSON.

Use a credential reference:

IntegrationConnection
        ↓
CredentialRecord
        ↓
Secret manager / encrypted store

Model:

class IntegrationCredential(Base):
    __tablename__ = "integration_credentials"

    id: Mapped[UUID] = mapped_column(
        PGUUID(as_uuid=True),
        primary_key=True,
        default=uuid4,
    )

    integration_id: Mapped[UUID] = mapped_column(
        PGUUID(as_uuid=True),
        ForeignKey(
            "integration_connections.id",
            ondelete="CASCADE",
        ),
        nullable=False,
    )

    secret_reference: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(
        String(500),
        nullable=False,
    )

    status: Mapped[CredentialStatus] = mapped_column(
        String(32),
        nullable=False,
    )

    expires_at: Mapped[datetime | None] = mapped_column(
        DateTime(timezone=True),
    )

    created_at: Mapped[datetime] = mapped_column(
        DateTime(timezone=True),
        nullable=False,
        server_default=text("CURRENT_TIMESTAMP"),
    )

secret_reference should point to:

AWS Secrets Manager
HashiCorp Vault
GCP Secret Manager
Azure Key Vault

or another production secret store.

Never return credentials through the API.

3.15.8 Monitoring definition example

A real configured monitoring rule might be:

{
  "query": {
    "resource": "deliveries",
    "filters": [
      {
        "field": "agreement_reference",
        "operator": "equals",
        "value_source": {
          "type": "AGREEMENT_FIELD",
          "path": "reference_number"
        }
      }
    ]
  },
  "evaluation": {
    "type": "EXISTENCE",
    "minimum_count": 1
  }
}

Notice:

agreement_reference

comes from the actual agreement.

It is not hardcoded.

3.15.9 Connector interface
connectors/base.py
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod
from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import datetime
from typing import Any


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ExternalObservation:

    external_id: str
    observed_at: datetime

    resource_type: str

    payload: dict[str, Any]

    source_reference: dict[str, Any]


class Connector(ABC):

    @abstractmethod
    async def validate_connection(
        self,
    ) -> bool:
        raise NotImplementedError

    @abstractmethod
    async def fetch(
        self,
        query: dict,
    ) -> list[ExternalObservation]:
        raise NotImplementedError

    @abstractmethod
    async def close(
        self,
    ) -> None:
        pass

No obligation-specific code belongs inside the connector.

3.15.10 Connector registry
class ConnectorRegistry:

    def __init__(self):
        self._connectors = {}

    def register(
        self,
        provider_key: str,
        connector_factory,
    ):
        self._connectors[provider_key] = (
            connector_factory
        )

    def create(
        self,
        provider_key: str,
        credentials,
        configuration,
    ):

        factory = self._connectors.get(
            provider_key
        )

        if factory is None:
            raise ValueError(
                f"Unsupported connector: {provider_key}"
            )

        return factory(
            credentials=credentials,
            configuration=configuration,
        )
3.15.11 Real-provider rule

Do not create:

FakeSalesforceConnector
MockERPConnector
DemoDeliveryConnector
SyntheticObservationProvider

as part of production application code.

For a provider that is not connected:

integration status = DISCONNECTED

and monitoring produces:

INCONCLUSIVE

rather than fake success/failure.

3.15.13 Payload hashing

Use the real external payload.

import hashlib
import json


def hash_payload(payload: dict) -> str:

    canonical = json.dumps(
        payload,
        sort_keys=True,
        separators=(",", ":"),
        ensure_ascii=False,
    )

    return hashlib.sha256(
        canonical.encode("utf-8")
    ).hexdigest()

This allows later verification that an observation has not been modified.

3.15.14 Observation deduplication

External APIs can return the same record repeatedly.

Use:

integration_id
+
monitoring_id
+
external_id
+
observed_at
+
payload_hash

for deduplication.

A retry must not create a different contractual event.

3.15.15 Evaluator interface
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod


class ObservationEvaluator(ABC):

    @abstractmethod
    async def evaluate(
        self,
        *,
        observations,
        definition,
    ):
        raise NotImplementedError

Implement evaluators independently.

3.15.16 Existence evaluator
class ExistenceEvaluator:

    async def evaluate(
        self,
        *,
        observations,
        definition,
    ):

        minimum = definition.get(
            "minimum_count",
            1,
        )

        count = len(observations)

        if count >= minimum:

            return {
                "result": "PASS",
                "metrics": {
                    "observed_count": count,
                    "required_count": minimum,
                },
            }

        return {
            "result": "FAIL",
            "metrics": {
                "observed_count": count,
                "required_count": minimum,
            },
        }

Do not put arbitrary contractual logic into an evaluator.

The evaluation definition must come from the configured monitoring rule.

3.15.17 Freshness evaluator

A useful operational condition is:

latest observation must not be older than configured interval

Configuration:

{
  "type": "FRESHNESS",
  "max_age": {
    "amount": 24,
    "unit": "HOUR"
  }
}

This is configuration, not a universal 24-hour rule.

3.15.18 Threshold evaluator

For a real source containing a numeric metric:

{
  "type": "THRESHOLD",
  "field": "delivered_units",
  "operator": "greater_than_or_equal",
  "value_source": {
    "type": "AGREEMENT_FIELD",
    "path": "required_quantity"
  }
}

The expected value comes from the actual agreement.

That prevents:

required_quantity = 100

from appearing in code.

3.15.19 Safe field resolver

Never allow:

eval(user_supplied_expression)

Use an allow-listed field resolver.

def resolve_path(
    data: dict,
    path: str,
):

    current = data

    for part in path.split("."):

        if not isinstance(current, dict):
            return None

        current = current.get(part)

    return current

Then validate allowed paths against a connector schema.

3.15.21 Why preserve evaluations?

Because external data changes.

Suppose:

08:00 → PASS
12:00 → FAIL

You need to know:

what source data existed
what rule was evaluated
what result was produced
when it happened

This is operational history.

3.15.22 Monitoring orchestration
service.py
class MonitoringService:

    async def execute(
        self,
        db,
        *,
        monitoring,
        integration,
        credentials,
    ):

        connector = self.registry.create(
            integration.provider_key,
            credentials,
            integration.configuration,
        )

        try:

            observations = await connector.fetch(
                monitoring.query_definition
            )

            stored = []

            for observation in observations:

                record = await self.store_observation(
                    db,
                    monitoring,
                    integration,
                    observation,
                )

                if record:
                    stored.append(record)

            evaluator = self.evaluators.get(
                monitoring.evaluation_definition["type"]
            )

            if evaluator is None:
                raise ValueError(
                    "Unsupported monitoring evaluator"
                )

            result = await evaluator.evaluate(
                observations=stored,
                definition=monitoring.evaluation_definition,
            )

            return await self.store_evaluation(
                db,
                monitoring=monitoring,
                result=result,
                observations=stored,
            )

        finally:
            await connector.close()
3.15.23 What happens after FAIL

A failed monitoring evaluation should not automatically mean:

CONTRACT BREACH

Instead:

Evaluation FAIL
     ↓
Operational exception
     ↓
Human review
     ↓
Possible contractual issue

This matches the approach from 3.13 and 3.14.

3.15.25 Monitoring failure versus source failure

These must remain separate.

Contract requirement failed
Source reachable
+
data retrieved
+
rule evaluated
+
result = FAIL

This is a genuine monitoring failure.

Integration unavailable
Source unavailable

This is:

INCONCLUSIVE

not:

FAIL

That distinction prevents false contract-risk alerts.

3.15.26 Connector health

Each integration should track:

last_success_at
last_failure_at
consecutive_failures
last_error_code
latency
credential_status

Example:

class IntegrationHealth(Base):
    __tablename__ = "integration_health"

    integration_id: Mapped[UUID] = mapped_column(
        PGUUID(as_uuid=True),
        ForeignKey(
            "integration_connections.id",
            ondelete="CASCADE",
        ),
        primary_key=True,
    )

    last_success_at: Mapped[datetime | None]
    last_failure_at: Mapped[datetime | None]

    consecutive_failures: Mapped[int]

    last_latency_ms: Mapped[int | None]

    last_error_code: Mapped[str | None]
3.15.27 Automatic disabling

Do not automatically disable a connector after an arbitrary hardcoded number of failures.

Instead use workspace/system configuration:

{
  "failure_policy": {
    "max_consecutive_failures": 5,
    "action": "PAUSE_MONITORING"
  }
}

Then:

failure threshold reached
        ↓
PAUSE
        ↓
notification
        ↓
operator fixes connection
        ↓
resume
3.15.28 Webhook support

For systems that support webhooks:

External system
      ↓
Webhook
      ↓
HTTPS endpoint
      ↓
Signature verification
      ↓
Raw event storage
      ↓
Normalization
      ↓
Observation
      ↓
Evaluation

Never process an unverified webhook as trusted data.

3.15.29 Webhook endpoint
@router.post(
    "/integrations/{integration_id}/webhook"
)
async def receive_webhook(
    integration_id: UUID,
    request: Request,
    db: AsyncSession = Depends(get_db),
):
    raw_body = await request.body()

    signature = request.headers.get(
        "X-Signature"
    )

    integration = await load_integration(
        db,
        integration_id,
    )

    await webhook_verifier.verify(
        integration=integration,
        raw_body=raw_body,
        signature=signature,
    )

    event = await webhook_service.persist(
        db,
        integration=integration,
        raw_body=raw_body,
    )

    await db.commit()

    return {
        "accepted": True,
        "event_id": event.id,
    }

The endpoint should return an event ID, not claim contractual fulfillment.

3.15.30 Replay protection

Webhook events need:

provider event ID
signature
timestamp
payload hash
received_at

Reject:

old timestamp
duplicate event ID
invalid signature

according to the connector's verified protocol.

3.15.31 API polling scheduler

For polling integrations:

Celery Beat
   ↓
due monitoring definitions
   ↓
worker
   ↓
connector
   ↓
observation
   ↓
evaluation

Do not create one Celery task per user indefinitely.

Use incremental scheduling.

3.15.32 Monitoring scheduler
async def schedule_due_monitoring(
    db,
    now,
):

    result = await db.execute(
        select(ObligationMonitoring)
        .where(
            ObligationMonitoring.status
            == "ACTIVE",
            # next_run_at <= now
        )
        .with_for_update(
            skip_locked=True
        )
    )

    return list(result.scalars())

Add:

next_run_at
last_run_at

to ObligationMonitoring.

3.15.33 Idempotent execution

Every run gets:

monitoring_run_id

and:

idempotency_key

Example:

monitoring_id + scheduled_period

A repeated worker invocation therefore does not create another logical monitoring result.

3.15.34 Monitoring run
class MonitoringRun(Base):
    __tablename__ = "monitoring_runs"

    id: Mapped[UUID] = mapped_column(
        PGUUID(as_uuid=True),
        primary_key=True,
        default=uuid4,
    )

    monitoring_id: Mapped[UUID] = mapped_column(

            ondelete="CASCADE",
        ),
        nullable=False,
    )

    organization_id: Mapped[UUID] = mapped_column(
        PGUUID(as_uuid=True),
        ForeignKey(
            "organizations.id",
            ondelete="CASCADE",
        ),
        nullable=False,
    )

    idempotency_key: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(
        String(500),
        nullable=False,
        unique=True,
    )

    status: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(
        String(32),
        nullable=False,
    )

    started_at: Mapped[datetime] = mapped_column(
        DateTime(timezone=True),
        nullable=False,
    )

    completed_at: Mapped[datetime | None] = mapped_column(
        DateTime(timezone=True),
    )

    error: Mapped[dict | None] = mapped_column(
        JSONB
    )
3.15.35 Linking monitoring to obligation instances

This is where 3.13 and 3.15 connect.

Agreement
   ↓
Obligation
   ↓
Obligation Instance
   ↓
Monitoring Run
   ↓
Observations
   ↓
Evaluation

For example:

Q2 report obligation instance
        ↓

        ↓
external system
        ↓
report found
        ↓
PASS
        ↓
instance can move toward COMPLETED
3.15.36 Automatic completion rules

Be conservative.

A PASS can automatically advance a task only if the obligation explicitly permits it.

Configuration:

{
  "automation": {
    "on_pass": "MARK_TASK_READY"
  }
}

Possible actions:

NO_ACTION
MARK_TASK_READY
ATTACH_EVIDENCE
COMPLETE_TASK

The workspace chooses the allowed behavior.

Do not universally auto-complete contractual obligations from one external observation.

3.15.37 Evidence generated from real observations

A monitoring result can become evidence:

External Observation
       ↓
Evidence Record
       ↓
Obligation Instance

Example:

{
  "evidence_type": "SYSTEM_RECORD",
  "value": {
    "integration_id": "...",
    "external_id": "...",
    "observation_id": "...",
    "payload_hash": "..."
  }
}

That gives you a traceable evidence chain.

3.15.38 External evidence integrity

For every evidence record store:

source
source identifier
observed_at
received_at
payload hash
integration ID
monitoring run ID

This makes it possible to reconstruct:

What external data caused the system to mark this obligation as satisfied?

3.15.42 Connector capability model

Each provider declares capabilities:

class ConnectorMetadata:

    provider_key: str

    capabilities: set[ConnectorCapability]

    configuration_schema: dict

    credential_schema: dict

For example:

Provider A

WEBHOOK

Provider B
READ

Provider C
READ
WRITE
WEBHOOK

Do not expose WRITE operations unless explicitly implemented and separately authorized.

3.15.43 Read-only by default

For this milestone, make all external monitoring connectors:

READ

by default.

The platform should not modify external systems merely because a contract has an overdue obligation.

Any future write capability should be its own security-reviewed milestone.

3.15.44 Data minimization

External integrations should fetch only the fields necessary for evaluation.

Avoid:

fetch entire ERP database

Prefer:

resource
+
specific fields
+
specific filters

Example:

{
  "resource": "deliveries",
  "fields": [
    "id",
    "agreement_reference",
    "delivery_date",
    "quantity"
  ]
}

This reduces exposure and processing risk.

3.15.45 External data retention

Observations may contain sensitive operational data.

Therefore configure:

retention policy
redaction policy
encryption
access policy

Raw data should not automatically live forever.

Hash/reference information can have a different retention period from raw payload.

3.15.46 Monitoring authorization

The user creating a monitoring integration must have:

organization administrator

or the configured integration-management permission.

Creating a monitoring rule requires:

obligation edit/workflow permission

Reading raw external observations should be more restricted than reading the summary.

For example:

Monitoring summary
    → can_view

Raw external payload
    → can_view_monitoring_data

3.15.55 API safety

Reject monitoring configurations that reference:

unknown field
unknown operator
unknown evaluator
unknown integration
wrong organization
wrong agreement version
inactive obligation

Never allow raw SQL queries or arbitrary code through the monitoring API.

3.15.56 Database constraints

Add constraints such as:

monitoring.organization_id
=
obligation.organization_id
=
agreement.organization_id
=
integration.organization_id

Application checks are required, but database-level constraints or composite foreign-key strategies should provide defense-in-depth where practical.

3.15.57 Version handling

This is another critical relationship:

Monitoring Definition
      ↓
Source Version

If Version 11 changes:

required_quantity

the existing monitoring definition must become stale.

Flow:

Version 11
   ↓
Version 12
   ↓
affected monitoring detected
   ↓
PAUSED / REQUIRES_REVIEW

Never continue evaluating against an outdated contractual rule.

3.15.58 Automatic recalculation after amendment

Connect the 3.11/3.12 outbox:

AGREEMENT_VERSION_FINALIZED
        ↓
detect affected obligations
        ↓
detect affected monitoring
        ↓
mark stale
        ↓
notify owner
        ↓
new configuration
        ↓
resume

This is safer than silently translating the old rule onto a changed contract.

What exact result?

That is:

  ↓

  ↓

  ↓

  ↓

  ↓

  ↓

This is the complete evidence graph.

3.16 — Contract Intelligence Graph, Cross-Agreement Dependencies & Entity-Level Risk

This milestone introduces the relationship layer that lets the platform reason across the entire contract portfolio instead of treating every agreement as isolated.

The central model becomes:

Party
  │
  ├── Agreement A
  │       ├── Obligation 1
  │       ├── Obligation 2
  │       ├── Document
  │       └── Risk Finding
  │
  ├── Agreement B
  │       ├── Obligation 3
  │       └── Risk Finding
  │
  └── Agreement C
          └── Amendment of Agreement A

That makes questions like these possible:

Which agreements depend on this supplier?
Which obligations are affected by this agreement amendment?
Which agreements share the same counterparty?
What risks concentrate around one entity?
What breaks if this dependency changes?
Which agreements are indirectly connected?

The graph is an intelligence layer. It does not replace the existing agreement, party, obligation, lifecycle, document, or risk tables.

3.16.1 Architecture
                         DOMAIN SYSTEM
                              │
        ┌─────────────────────┼─────────────────────┐
        ▼                     ▼                     ▼
   Agreements             Parties               Obligations
        │                     │                     │
        ├──────────────┬──────┴─────────────┬──────┤
        ▼              ▼                    ▼      ▼
    Documents       Lifecycle             Risks   Templates
        │              │                    │
        └──────────────┴──────────┬─────────┘
                                  ▼
                         GRAPH PROJECTION
                                  │
                     ┌────────────┴────────────┐
                     ▼                         ▼
               Graph Nodes                Graph Edges
                     │                         │
                     └────────────┬────────────┘
                                  ▼
                        Graph Query Engine
                                  │
             ┌────────────────────┼───────────────────┐
             ▼                    ▼                   ▼
       Impact Analysis       Dependency Map      Entity Risk
             │                    │                   │
             └────────────────────┼───────────────────┘
                                  ▼
                        Dashboard / API / Alerts
3.16.2 Do not make the graph the system of record

This is important.

The graph should reference:

agreements
parties
obligations
documents
risk findings
versions

rather than copying all their business data into the graph.

For example:

graph node
    ↓
agreement_id
    ↓
agreements table

Therefore the authoritative agreement title, status, version, etc. remains in the existing agreement domain.

3.16.5 Graph node model
# backend/app/graph/models.py

from datetime import datetime
from uuid import UUID, uuid4

from sqlalchemy import (
    DateTime,
    ForeignKey,
    Index,
    String,
    UniqueConstraint,
    text,
)
from sqlalchemy.dialects.postgresql import UUID as PGUUID, JSONB
from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped, mapped_column

from app.db.base import Base

from .enums import (
    GraphNodeType,
    GraphEdgeType,
    GraphEdgeStatus,
    GraphSourceType,
    GraphConfidence,
)


class GraphNode(Base):
    __tablename__ = "graph_nodes"

    id: Mapped[UUID] = mapped_column(
        PGUUID(as_uuid=True),
        primary_key=True,
        default=uuid4,
    )

    organization_id: Mapped[UUID] = mapped_column(
        PGUUID(as_uuid=True),
        ForeignKey(
            "organizations.id",
            ondelete="CASCADE",
        ),
        nullable=False,
    )

    node_type: Mapped[GraphNodeType] = mapped_column(
        String(64),
        nullable=False,
    )

    object_id: Mapped[UUID] = mapped_column(
        PGUUID(as_uuid=True),
        nullable=False,
    )

    metadata: Mapped[dict] = mapped_column(
        JSONB,
        nullable=False,
        default=dict,
    )

    created_at: Mapped[datetime] = mapped_column(
        DateTime(timezone=True),
        nullable=False,
        server_default=text("CURRENT_TIMESTAMP"),
    )

    updated_at: Mapped[datetime] = mapped_column(
        DateTime(timezone=True),
        nullable=False,
        server_default=text("CURRENT_TIMESTAMP"),
    )

    __table_args__ = (
        UniqueConstraint(
            "organization_id",
            "node_type",
            "object_id",
            name="uq_graph_node_object",
        ),
        Index(
            "ix_graph_nodes_object",
            "organization_id",
            "object_id",
        ),
    )


class GraphEdge(Base):
    __tablename__ = "graph_edges"

    id: Mapped[UUID] = mapped_column(
        PGUUID(as_uuid=True),
        primary_key=True,
        default=uuid4,
    )

    organization_id: Mapped[UUID] = mapped_column(
        PGUUID(as_uuid=True),
        ForeignKey(
            "organizations.id",
            ondelete="CASCADE",
        ),
        nullable=False,
    )

    source_node_id: Mapped[UUID] = mapped_column(
        PGUUID(as_uuid=True),
        nullable=False,
    )

    target_node_id: Mapped[UUID] = mapped_column(
        PGUUID(as_uuid=True),
        nullable=False,
    )

    edge_type: Mapped[GraphEdgeType] = mapped_column(
        String(100),
        nullable=False,
    )

    status: Mapped[GraphEdgeStatus] = mapped_column(
        String(32),
        nullable=False,
        default=GraphEdgeStatus.ACTIVE,
    )

    source_version_id: Mapped[UUID | None] = mapped_column(
        PGUUID(as_uuid=True),
        ForeignKey("agreement_versions.id"),
    )

    source_type: Mapped[GraphSourceType] = mapped_column(
        String(32),
        nullable=False,
    )

    confidence: Mapped[GraphConfidence] = mapped_column(
        String(32),
        nullable=False,
    )

    source_reference: Mapped[dict] = mapped_column(
        JSONB,
        nullable=False,
    )

    properties: Mapped[dict] = mapped_column(
        JSONB,
        nullable=False,
        default=dict,
    )

    created_at: Mapped[datetime] = mapped_column(
        DateTime(timezone=True),
        nullable=False,
        server_default=text("CURRENT_TIMESTAMP"),
    )

    updated_at: Mapped[datetime] = mapped_column(
        DateTime(timezone=True),
        nullable=False,
        server_default=text("CURRENT_TIMESTAMP"),
    )

    __table_args__ = (
        Index(
            "ix_graph_edges_source",
            "organization_id",
            "source_node_id",
            "status",
        ),
        Index(
            "ix_graph_edges_target",
            "organization_id",
            "target_node_id",
            "status",
        ),
        Index(
            "ix_graph_edges_type",
            "organization_id",
            "edge_type",
            "status",
        ),
    )
3.16.6 Tenant isolation inside the graph

A graph is especially dangerous for multi-tenant isolation because a single traversal could accidentally cross workspaces.

The graph must therefore enforce:

edge.organization_id
    ==
source_node.organization_id
    ==
target_node.organization_id

Use composite foreign keys.

Update the model:

from sqlalchemy import ForeignKeyConstraint


class GraphEdge(Base):

    # ...

    __table_args__ = (
        ForeignKeyConstraint(
            [
                "organization_id",
                "source_node_id",
            ],
            [
                "graph_nodes.organization_id",
                "graph_nodes.id",
            ],
        ),

        ForeignKeyConstraint(
            [
                "organization_id",
                "target_node_id",
            ],
            [
                "graph_nodes.organization_id",
                "graph_nodes.id",
            ],
        ),

        Index(
            "ix_graph_edges_source",
            "organization_id",
            "source_node_id",
            "status",
        ),

        Index(
            "ix_graph_edges_target",
            "organization_id",
            "target_node_id",
            "status",
        ),
    )

Now PostgreSQL itself rejects an edge joining nodes from different organizations.

This is much stronger than relying solely on Python checks.

3.16.7 Node creation

The graph projector should create a node when a domain object becomes relevant.

from sqlalchemy import select


async def get_or_create_node(
    db,
    *,
    organization_id,
    node_type,
    object_id,
    metadata=None,
):

    result = await db.execute(
        select(GraphNode)
        .where(
            GraphNode.organization_id == organization_id,
            GraphNode.node_type == node_type,
            GraphNode.object_id == object_id,
        )
    )

    node = result.scalar_one_or_none()

    if node:
        return node

    node = GraphNode(
        organization_id=organization_id,
        node_type=node_type,
        object_id=object_id,
        metadata=metadata or {},
    )

    db.add(node)

    await db.flush()

    return node
3.16.8 Creating edges

Centralize edge creation.

from sqlalchemy import select


class GraphEdgeService:

    async def create_edge(
        self,
        db,
        *,
        organization_id,
        source_node_id,
        target_node_id,
        edge_type,
        source_version_id=None,
        source_type,
        confidence,
        source_reference,
        properties=None,
    ):

        existing = await db.execute(
            select(GraphEdge)
            .where(
                GraphEdge.organization_id
                == organization_id,

                GraphEdge.source_node_id
                == source_node_id,

                GraphEdge.target_node_id
                == target_node_id,

                GraphEdge.edge_type
                == edge_type,

                GraphEdge.status
                == GraphEdgeStatus.ACTIVE,
            )
        )

        edge = existing.scalar_one_or_none()

        if edge:
            return edge

        edge = GraphEdge(
            organization_id=organization_id,
            source_node_id=source_node_id,
            target_node_id=target_node_id,
            edge_type=edge_type,
            status=GraphEdgeStatus.ACTIVE,
            source_version_id=source_version_id,
            source_type=source_type,
            confidence=confidence,
            source_reference=source_reference,
            properties=properties or {},
        )

        db.add(edge)

        await db.flush()

        return edge
3.16.9 Domain projection

The graph should be populated from domain events, not from frontend requests.

For example:

AGREEMENT_CREATED
      ↓
graph projector
      ↓
AGREEMENT node

AGREEMENT_VERSION_CREATED
      ↓
VERSION node
      ↓
AGREEMENT_HAS_VERSION edge

AGREEMENT_PARTY_LINKED
      ↓
PARTY node
      ↓
AGREEMENT_HAS_PARTY edge

OBLIGATION_CREATED
      ↓
OBLIGATION node
      ↓
AGREEMENT_HAS_OBLIGATION edge

RISK_FINDING_CREATED
      ↓
RISK node
      ↓
AGREEMENT_HAS_RISK edge

This keeps the graph synchronized with the domain.

3.16.10 Projector
projector.py
class ContractGraphProjector:

    async def project(
        self,
        db,
        event,
    ):

        handlers = {
            "AGREEMENT_CREATED": self._agreement_created,
            "AGREEMENT_VERSION_CREATED": (
                self._agreement_version_created
            ),
            "AGREEMENT_PARTY_LINKED": (
                self._agreement_party_linked
            ),
            "OBLIGATION_CREATED": (
                self._obligation_created
            ),
            "RISK_FINDING_CREATED": (
                self._risk_created
            ),
            "AGREEMENT_AMENDED": (
                self._agreement_amended
            ),
        }

        handler = handlers.get(event.event_type)

        if handler:
            await handler(db, event)

The outbox already established in previous milestones becomes the event transport.

3.16.16 Agreement-to-agreement dependencies

Some agreements depend on other agreements.

Examples include:

Master agreement
      ↓
Statement of Work

Framework agreement
      ↓
Order agreement

Data processing agreement
      ↓
Services agreement

These relationships should be explicit.

Create:

AGREEMENT_DEPENDS_ON
AGREEMENT_AMENDS
AGREEMENT_REFERENCES

Do not use one generic RELATED_TO relationship. It loses semantic meaning.

3.16.17 Dependency creation

A user can explicitly create:

{
  "target_agreement_id": "...",
  "relationship": "AGREEMENT_DEPENDS_ON",
  "source_reference": {
    "block_id": "..."
  }
}

Server validates:

same workspace
+
both agreements exist
+
user can edit source agreement
+
target agreement visible to user
+
relationship permitted
3.16.18 AI-discovered relationships

Later, semantic analysis may detect:

Agreement B appears to reference Agreement A.

That must be stored differently:

source_type = AI
confidence = MEDIUM

and:

status = CANDIDATE

rather than immediately becoming a verified dependency.

Extend status:

class GraphEdgeReviewStatus(StrEnum):
    AUTO_VERIFIED = "AUTO_VERIFIED"
    REVIEW_REQUIRED = "REVIEW_REQUIRED"
    CONFIRMED = "CONFIRMED"
    REJECTED = "REJECTED"

Then:

AI detection
    ↓
candidate edge
    ↓
human review
    ↓
confirmed/rejected
3.16.19 Graph confidence

Use confidence only to describe the relationship's certainty.

It must not be mistaken for legal importance.

For example:

Relationship:
Agreement B references Agreement A

Confidence:
HIGH

This means the system is confident the relationship exists.

It does not mean the relationship is legally significant.

3.16.20 Graph traversal

The first implementation can use PostgreSQL recursive CTEs.

No graph database is required yet.

traversal.py
from sqlalchemy import text


async def traverse(
    db,
    *,
    organization_id,
    start_node_id,
    max_depth=5,
):

    query = text(
        """
        WITH RECURSIVE graph_walk AS (

            SELECT
                ge.target_node_id AS node_id,
                1 AS depth,
                ARRAY[
                    ge.source_node_id,
                    ge.target_node_id
                ] AS path
            FROM graph_edges ge
            WHERE
                ge.organization_id = :organization_id
                AND ge.source_node_id = :start_node_id
                AND ge.status = 'ACTIVE'

            UNION ALL

            SELECT
                ge.target_node_id,
                gw.depth + 1,
                gw.path || ge.target_node_id
            FROM graph_walk gw
            JOIN graph_edges ge
                ON ge.source_node_id = gw.node_id
            WHERE
                ge.organization_id = :organization_id
                AND ge.status = 'ACTIVE'
                AND gw.depth < :max_depth
                AND NOT ge.target_node_id = ANY(gw.path)
        )

        SELECT
            node_id,
            depth,
            path
        FROM graph_walk
        ORDER BY depth, node_id
        """
    )

    result = await db.execute(
        query,
        {
            "organization_id": organization_id,
            "start_node_id": start_node_id,
            "max_depth": max_depth,
        },
    )

    return result.mappings().all()

The cycle protection:

NOT ge.target_node_id = ANY(gw.path)

prevents graph loops from exploding the query.

3.16.21 Traversal must be bounded

Never expose:

max_depth = unlimited

to an API request.

Use a configured system maximum:

GRAPH_MAX_TRAVERSAL_DEPTH = ...

and validate the client value against it.

This is an operational configuration value, not contractual data.

3.16.22 Impact analysis

Now create:

class ImpactAnalysisService:

    async def analyze_node(

        organization_id,

        paths = await traverse(
            db,

            start_node_id=node_id,
            max_depth=max_depth,

            db,

3.16.26 Entity risk aggregation

For a party:

Party
 ↓
all connected agreements
 ↓
their open risk findings
 ↓
aggregation

The service should ignore:

DISMISSED
SUPERSEDED

findings unless the policy explicitly includes them.

3.16.27 Entity risk service
class EntityRiskService:

    async def rebuild(
        self,
        db,
        *,
        organization_id,
        node_id,
        policy,
    ):

        finding_ids = await self._resolve_connected_findings(
            db,
            organization_id=organization_id,
            node_id=node_id,
        )

        findings = await self._load_findings(
            db,
            finding_ids,
        )

        active = [
            finding
            for finding in findings
            if finding.status
            not in {
                "DISMISSED",
                "SUPERSEDED",
            }
        ]

        profile = await self._calculate(
            active,
            policy,
        )

        await self._persist_profile(
            db,
            organization_id=organization_id,
            node_id=node_id,
            profile=profile,
            policy_version=policy["version"],
        )

        return profile
3.16.28 Do not double-count risks

This is a common graph mistake.

Suppose:

Agreement A
   ↓
Obligation 1
   ↓
Risk Finding X

A traversal must not count X three times simply because there are multiple paths to it.

Deduplicate by:

unique_finding_ids = {
    finding.id
    for finding in findings
}

Entity risk should be based on unique risk findings.

3.16.29 Relationship importance

Not every relationship has equal impact.

A configurable relationship weight can help impact ranking:

{
  "edge_weights": {
    "AGREEMENT_DEPENDS_ON": 1.0,
    "AGREEMENT_HAS_PARTY": 0.8,
    "AGREEMENT_HAS_OBLIGATION": 0.7,
    "OBLIGATION_RESPONSIBLE_PARTY": 0.9
  }
}

This belongs to graph policy/configuration.

Do not bake legal assumptions into these values.

3.16.36 Graph snapshot hash

For reproducibility, compute a hash over the graph inputs used by an analysis.

For example:

node IDs
+
edge IDs
+
edge statuses
+
source versions

canonicalized and hashed.

import hashlib
import json


def graph_snapshot_hash(
    node_ids,
    edges,
):

    payload = {
        "nodes": sorted(
            str(node_id)
            for node_id in node_ids
        ),
        "edges": sorted(
            [
                {
                    "id": str(edge.id),
                    "source": str(edge.source_node_id),
                    "target": str(edge.target_node_id),
                    "type": edge.edge_type,
                    "status": edge.status,
                }
                for edge in edges
            ],
            key=lambda x: x["id"],
        ),
    }

    canonical = json.dumps(
        payload,
        sort_keys=True,
        separators=(",", ":"),
    )

    return hashlib.sha256(
        canonical.encode()
    ).hexdigest()

That lets you reconstruct what the impact analysis actually saw.

3.16.37 Graph integrity checker

Because graph edges are projections, they need periodic validation.

Create:

class GraphIntegrityService:

    async def verify(
        self,
        db,
        *,
        organization_id,
    ):

        problems = []

        # Example:
        # Graph agreement node must point to
        # an existing agreement in the same organization.

        problems.extend(
            await self._verify_agreements(
                db,
                organization_id,
            )
        )

        problems.extend(
            await self._verify_obligations(
                db,
                organization_id,
            )
        )

        problems.extend(
            await self._verify_edges(
                db,
                organization_id,
            )
        )

        return problems
3.16.38 Repair strategy

Never silently repair graph inconsistencies inside a normal user request.

Use:

detect
 ↓
audit
 ↓
repair job
 ↓
rebuild projection

The graph can be safely rebuilt from domain state.

This is another reason the domain tables remain authoritative.

3.16.39 Full graph rebuild

Create an administrative operation:

POST /api/admin/graph/rebuild

The system admin must explicitly authorize it.

Process:

clear stale projection
      ↓
read actual domain records
      ↓
recreate graph nodes
      ↓
recreate verified edges
      ↓
reprocess confirmed derived relationships
      ↓
integrity verification

No business data is invented during the rebuild.

3.16.43 Authorization

Graph access must not bypass existing agreement permissions.

For example, a user who can see Agreement A but not Agreement B must not be able to learn Agreement B's sensitive metadata just because A has a graph edge to B.

Therefore:

Graph edge exists
      ↓
destination authorization
      ↓
visible?
   /     \
 YES      NO
  │        │
show     redact

The safest default is to exclude unauthorized nodes entirely.

3.16.44 Graph endpoint implementation
async def visible_neighbors(
    db,
    user,
    node_id,
):

    raw = await graph_service.neighbors(
        db,
        user.organization_id,
        node_id,
    )

    visible = []

    for item in raw:

        if await graph_authorizer.can_view(
            db,
            user=user,
            node=item,
        ):
            visible.append(item)

    return visible

For large graphs, optimize authorization using set-based DB queries rather than one authorization query per node.

Do not ship an N+1 authorization query architecture.

Score: 78

──────────────────────

And allow the user to trace each one back to:

3.16.49 Entity risk is not legal risk

Label it clearly:

PORTFOLIO ENTITY RISK

rather than:

LEGAL LIABILITY SCORE

unless a qualified legal/risk methodology has actually been configured and approved.

3.16.50 Cross-agreement analytics

The graph enables portfolio-level queries.

Shared parties
Party
 ↓
agreements
 ↓
count
Agreements with common obligations
Agreement A
   ↓
Party X

Agreement B
   ↓

Dependency chains
A → depends on B → depends on C
Risk propagation

Then:

3.16.51 Risk propagation must not automatically invent risk

If Agreement A has a risk:

Risk A

and Agreement B depends on A, do not automatically create:

Risk B

Instead record:

Potential inherited exposure

only when a configured rule establishes that relationship.

This distinction prevents graph traversal from becoming a risk-hallucination engine.

3.16.52 Impact rules

Create configurable policies:

class ImpactPolicy(Base):
    __tablename__ = "impact_policies"

    id: Mapped[UUID] = mapped_column(
        PGUUID(as_uuid=True),
        primary_key=True,
        default=uuid4,
    )

    organization_id: Mapped[UUID] = mapped_column(
        PGUUID(as_uuid=True),
        ForeignKey(
            "organizations.id",
            ondelete="CASCADE",
        ),
        nullable=False,
    )

    version: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(
        nullable=False
    )

    configuration: Mapped[dict] = mapped_column(
        JSONB,
        nullable=False,
    )

    active: Mapped[bool] = mapped_column(
        nullable=False,
    )

Example policy:

{
  "propagation": [
    {
      "from": "AGREEMENT_DEPENDS_ON",
      "to": "AGREEMENT",
      "enabled": true
    }
  ]
}

Again, these are operational/business policies created by the organization.

3.16.54 Graph event projection

The graph should subscribe to the existing outbox.

Agreement event
       ↓
Outbox
       ↓
Graph projector
       ↓
Graph mutation
       ↓
Activity/audit

Graph projection should itself be idempotent.

3.16.55 Projection idempotency

Use a processed-event record:

class GraphProjectionEvent(Base):
    __tablename__ = "graph_projection_events"

    event_id: Mapped[UUID] = mapped_column(
        PGUUID(as_uuid=True),
        primary_key=True,
    )

    organization_id: Mapped[UUID] = mapped_column(
        PGUUID(as_uuid=True),
        nullable=False,
    )

    processed_at: Mapped[datetime] = mapped_column(
        DateTime(timezone=True),
        nullable=False,
    )

Processing:

async def process_event(db, event):

    existing = await db.get(
        GraphProjectionEvent,
        event.id,
    )

    if existing:
        return

    await projector.project(
        db,
        event,
    )

    db.add(
        GraphProjectionEvent(
            event_id=event.id,
            organization_id=event.organization_id,
            processed_at=datetime.now(timezone.utc),
        )
    )

Everything happens inside one transaction.

3.16.56 Graph rebuild versus incremental projection

Use both.

Normal operation
domain event
 ↓
incremental projection
Recovery/integrity
full rebuild

This gives you resilience if a projection worker fails.

3.16.57 Graph stale detection

The graph should track the domain version it reflects.

For an agreement node:

graph.current_version_id

or derive it from version edges.

After an amendment:

agreement current version = 12
graph projected version = 11

The node is stale.

Then:

GRAPH_RECALCULATION_REQUIRED

and the projector catches up.

3.16.58 Cross-agreement dependency validation

Before accepting:

Agreement A → depends on → Agreement B

check:

both exist
both same organization
both visible
not same node
relationship allowed
no prohibited cycle if policy forbids it
source reference valid

Cycles are not automatically illegal.

For example:

A → references → B
B → references → A

may be legitimate.

Do not assume every cycle is an error.

3.16.59 Dependency cycle analysis

For AGREEMENT_DEPENDS_ON, a cycle may be operationally problematic.

Before accepting an explicit dependency:

A → B

check whether:

B → ... → A

already exists.

If yes:

return 409

with:

DEPENDENCY_CYCLE_DETECTED

unless the configured policy explicitly permits it.

3.16.60 Example dependency-cycle check
async def would_create_cycle(
    db,
    *,
    organization_id,
    source_node_id,
    target_node_id,
):

    reachable = await traverse(
        db,
        organization_id=organization_id,
        start_node_id=target_node_id,
        max_depth=100,
    )

    return any(
        row["node_id"] == source_node_id
        for row in reachable
    )

For large graphs, replace this with a more efficient reachability/indexing strategy.

3.16.61 Performance strategy

PostgreSQL recursive CTEs are a strong starting point.

Use indexes on:

organization_id
source_node_id
target_node_id
edge_type
status

Do not prematurely deploy Neo4j or another graph DB.

Move to a specialized graph store when actual workload demonstrates a need.

The graph abstraction lets you migrate later without changing the domain model.

3.16.62 Caching

Useful cache keys:

graph:neighbors:{org}:{node}
graph:impact:{org}:{root}:{snapshot}
entity-risk:{org}:{node}:{policy}

Invalidate when:

graph edge changes
risk finding changes
agreement version changes
party relationship changes
obligation changes

Redis can handle this.

Cached results are never authoritative.

3.16.63 API authorization example
@router.get(
    "/agreements/{agreement_id}/graph"
)
async def agreement_graph(
    agreement_id: UUID,
    db: AsyncSession = Depends(get_db),
    user=Depends(get_current_user),
):

    agreement = await require_agreement_permission(
        db,
        user=user,
        agreement_id=agreement_id,
        permission="can_view",
    )

    return await graph_service.for_agreement(
        db,
        user=user,
        agreement=agreement,
    )

The graph service then filters every returned node through authorization.

3.16.73 Security rules

The graph is potentially one of the highest-sensitivity interfaces in the platform.

Never allow:

GET /api/graph?organization_id=...

and trust the organization ID supplied by the client.

Always derive organization context from:

authenticated user
+
workspace membership

Also:

No cross-workspace traversals
No cross-workspace edges
No unauthorized node enumeration
No hidden-object leakage
No raw graph SQL from clients

3.16.75 Graph projection worker
from celery import shared_task


@shared_task(
    bind=True,
    autoretry_for=(Exception,),
    retry_backoff=True,
    max_retries=8,
)
def project_graph_event(
    self,
    event_id: str,
):

    import asyncio

    asyncio.run(
        _project_graph_event(event_id)
    )


async def _project_graph_event(event_id):

    from app.db.session import async_session_factory
    from app.events.repository import get_outbox_event

    async with async_session_factory() as db:

        event = await get_outbox_event(
            db,
            event_id,
        )

        if event is None:
            return

        await graph_projector.project(
            db,
            event,
        )

        await mark_graph_event_processed(
            db,
            event,
        )

        await db.commit()

The projection remains asynchronous and retryable.

3.17 — Contract Portfolio Intelligence, Advanced Analytics & Executive Decision Dashboard

Until now, the platform has become very good at understanding and operating on an individual agreement and its connected entities.

3.17 moves up one level:

Individual Contract Intelligence
            ↓
Portfolio Intelligence
            ↓
Decision Support

The goal is not to create another reporting page with arbitrary charts.

It should answer:

What is happening across the contract portfolio, what is changing, where is exposure concentrating, what requires attention, and why?

Every metric must remain traceable to actual underlying records.

3.17.2 Core principles

The analytics layer must follow six rules.

1. No invented business data

No:

fake agreements
fake risk scores
fake renewal dates
sample companies
synthetic portfolio statistics
2. No hidden calculation logic

Every KPI has a documented calculation.

3. Metrics are snapshots, not facts

A dashboard number such as:

87%

must have:

calculated_at
calculation_policy_version
data_window
source scope
4. Historical metrics must remain reproducible

If the source data changes, the system should be able to explain why the metric changed.

5. No AI-generated KPI without supporting facts

AI can explain data.

It cannot fabricate the underlying metric.

6. Portfolio analytics must respect workspace isolation

A user must never see another organization's aggregated metrics.

3.17.6 Metric definitions

Do not scatter KPI calculations throughout route handlers.

Create a metric registry.

from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Callable


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class MetricDefinition:

    key: str
    category: MetricCategory

    value_type: MetricValueType

    description: str

    calculator: Callable

Registry:

class MetricRegistry:

    def __init__(self):

        self._definitions = {}

    def register(
        self,
        definition: MetricDefinition,
    ):
        self._definitions[
            definition.key
        ] = definition

    def get(
        self,
        key: str,
    ):
        return self._definitions[key]

    def all(self):
        return list(
            self._definitions.values()
        )

3.17.8 Agreement inventory metrics
metrics/agreements.py
from sqlalchemy import select, func

from app.agreements.models import Agreement


async def active_agreements(
    db,
    organization_id,
):

    result = await db.execute(
        select(
            func.count(Agreement.id)
        )
        .where(
            Agreement.organization_id
            == organization_id,

            Agreement.archived_at.is_(None),
        )
    )

    return result.scalar_one()

No status assumptions beyond the actual domain schema.

3.17.9 Status distribution
async def agreement_status_distribution(
    db,
    organization_id,
):

    result = await db.execute(
        select(
            Agreement.status,
            func.count(Agreement.id),
        )
        .where(
            Agreement.organization_id
            == organization_id
        )
        .group_by(
            Agreement.status
        )
    )

    return {
        str(status): count
        for status, count in result.all()
    }
3.17.10 Lifecycle portfolio metrics

Connect 3.12.

async def expiring_agreement_count(
    db,
    organization_id,
):

    result = await db.execute(
        select(
            func.count(AgreementLifecycle.id)
        )
        .where(
            AgreementLifecycle.organization_id
            == organization_id,

            AgreementLifecycle.current_state
            == LifecycleState.EXPIRING,
        )
    )

    return result.scalar_one()

The metric follows lifecycle state already calculated from actual contract terms.

3.17.11 Renewal exposure

A useful metric is not simply:

renewals = 15

Instead distinguish:

renewals due
renewals pending decision
renewals decided
non-renewals
renewals with missing configuration

This lets executives distinguish known workload from unknown contractual state.

3.17.12 Missing-data visibility

One of the most useful portfolio metrics is:

Lifecycle completeness

Example:

Expiry date known              93%
Renewal rule known             87%
Notice period known            79%
Responsible owner assigned     96%

This tells users where the system's knowledge is incomplete.

Do not convert missing information into a false zero.

3.17.13 Data completeness model

Create:

class DataQualityMetric(Base):
    __tablename__ = "analytics_data_quality"

    id: Mapped[UUID] = mapped_column(
        PGUUID(as_uuid=True),

Then:

percentage = (
    numerator / denominator * 100
    if denominator
    else None
)
3.17.14 Obligation performance metrics

From 3.13:

completion rate
on-time rate
late rate
exception rate
evidence rejection rate
average delay
open workload

Use actual historical instances.

Example:

async def obligation_completion_rate(
    db,
    organization_id,
):

    total = await count_instances(
        db,
        organization_id,
    )

    completed = await count_completed_instances(
        db,
        organization_id,
    )

    if total == 0:
        return None

    return completed / total * 100

No denominator means no rate.

3.17.16 Concentration analysis

Portfolio concentration is useful for:

supplier dependence
customer dependence
counterparty exposure
operational dependency
risk concentration

But the system must use configurable policy.

Example:

{
  "concentration_policy": {
    "basis": "AGREEMENT_COUNT",
    "threshold": 0.25
  }
}

This means the workspace has chosen its definition.

The platform should not assert that 25% is universally dangerous.

3.17.17 Concentration metric
def concentration_share(
    entity_count: int,
    total_count: int,
):

    if total_count == 0:
        return None

    return entity_count / total_count

For financial exposure:

contract value

must only be aggregated where the agreement has an actual normalized monetary value.

No currency conversion should happen without a real exchange-rate source.

3.17.18 Currency normalization

Agreement value
       ↓

Example:

async def risk_category_distribution(
    db,
    organization_id,
):

    result = await db.execute(
        select(
            RiskFinding.category,
            func.count(RiskFinding.id),
        )
        .where(
            RiskFinding.organization_id
            == organization_id,

            RiskFinding.status.notin_([
                "DISMISSED",
                "SUPERSEDED",
            ]),
        )
        .group_by(
            RiskFinding.category
        )
    )

    return {
        str(category): count
        for category, count in result.all()
    }

3.17.25 Portfolio analytics service
class PortfolioAnalyticsService:

    async def calculate_dashboard(
        self,
        db,
        *,
        organization_id,
        scope,
    ):

        metrics = {}

        definitions = self.registry.all()

        for definition in definitions:

            metrics[definition.key] = await (
                definition.calculator(
                    db,
                    organization_id,
                    scope,
                )
            )

        return metrics

Do not run expensive calculations one-by-one if the dashboard becomes large.

Batch and materialize expensive metrics.

3.17.27 Why daily snapshots?

A historical chart should not depend on today's database state.

Example:

3.17.28 Anomaly detection

Now add actual anomaly detection over historical metrics.

Not:

AI thinks something looks strange.

Instead:

metric history
   ↓
statistical baseline
   ↓
deviation
   ↓
anomaly candidate

Start with explainable statistical methods.

3.17.29 Rolling baseline
from statistics import mean, pstdev


def detect_zscore(
    values: list[float],
    current: float,
    threshold: float = 3.0,
):

    if len(values) < 2:
        return None

    avg = mean(values)
    deviation = pstdev(values)

    if deviation == 0:
        return None

    z = (
        current - avg
    ) / deviation

    return {
        "z_score": z,
        "is_anomaly": abs(z) >= threshold,
    }

Do not use 3.0 as a contractual or business rule. It is an algorithmic parameter and should be part of the analytics policy.

3.17.30 Robust anomaly detection

Real contract portfolios may not follow normal distributions.

Also implement robust methods later:

median absolute deviation
percentile shifts
change-point detection
seasonal baseline

Use whichever method is configured for the metric.

3.17.33 Forecasting

Forecasting should only be enabled where enough actual historical data exists.

For example:

renewals expected next quarter
obligation workload expected
risk workload expected
document review workload expected

If history is insufficient:

Forecast unavailable
Insufficient historical observations

not a fabricated forecast.

3.17.34 Forecast interface
class ForecastResult:

    metric_key: str

    horizon: dict

    predictions: list[dict]

    confidence_interval: list[dict]

    training_window: dict

    method: str

For a future ML implementation, the model version must be recorded.

3.17.35 No prediction without training data

Do not implement:

forecast = model.predict(
    fake_training_data
)

There should be an explicit eligibility check:

if historical_count < minimum_required:
    return ForecastUnavailable(
        reason="INSUFFICIENT_HISTORY"
    )

3.17.48 Portfolio health

A portfolio health calculation should combine actual measurable dimensions.

For example:

portfolio health
    ↓
weighted:
risk
obligations

workflow backlog

Don't write:

risk * 0.4
obligations * 0.3

without making the methodology configurable.

3.17.49 Decision queue

Executives do not need every record first.

Create a prioritized action queue:

URGENT
Critical open risk

HIGH
Renewal decision approaching deadline

HIGH
Repeated obligation failure

MEDIUM
Lifecycle information incomplete

LOW
Integration health degradation

Priority must be derived from actual policy and evidence.

3.17.50 Decision priority engine
class DecisionPriorityService:

    def calculate(
        self,
        *,
        severity,
        deadline_distance,
        affected_entities,
        policy,
    ):

        weights = policy["weights"]

        score = (
            weights["severity"]
            * policy["severity_scores"][severity]
        )

        if deadline_distance is not None:
            score += (
                weights["deadline"]
                * deadline_distance
            )

        score += (
            weights["affected_entities"]
            * affected_entities
        )

        return round(score)

This becomes a policy-driven queue rather than arbitrary sorting.

3.17.55 Metric endpoint
@router.get(
    "/portfolio/metrics/{metric_key}"
)
async def get_metric(
    metric_key: str,
    db: AsyncSession = Depends(get_db),
    user=Depends(get_current_user),
):

    organization_id = await resolve_workspace(
        db,
        user,
    )

    definition = metric_registry.get(
        metric_key
    )

    if definition is None:
        raise HTTPException(
            status_code=404,
            detail="Metric not found",
        )

    return await analytics_service.calculate(
        db,
        organization_id=organization_id,
        metric=definition,
    )

Metric keys must come from the registry.

Never turn a client string into a SQL expression.

3.17.58 Background processing

Use Celery for:

historical trend calculations
